title: The Danish Way of Parenting
author: Jessica Joelle Alexander and Iben Dissing Sandahl
theme: Denmark's consistently high happiness rankings owe much to how children are raised, through free play, honesty, gentle reframing, empathy, calm respect and warm family togetherness.
takeaway: This week, plan one unhurried, screen-free family evening where everyone helps cook, plays a simple game, and agrees to leave complaints and arguments aside for those few hours.
summary: Denmark regularly appears near the top of world happiness surveys. Jessica Alexander, an American married to a Dane, and Iben Sandahl, a Danish psychotherapist, wondered whether the secret lay partly in how Danish children are raised. Their answer is a set of everyday habits, which they arrange under the word PARENT.

P stands for play. Danish children get plenty of free, unstructured time, often outdoors, to invent games, take small risks and settle their own disagreements. The authors argue that this builds resilience, self-control and confidence far better than a crowded timetable of lessons and screens.

A stands for authenticity. Children are encouraged to know and name their real feelings, including sad ones, and stories with difficult endings are shared rather than avoided. Praise focuses on effort and process instead of labels like clever, so children learn to value growth over image.

R stands for reframing. Danes tend to practise a realistic optimism, noticing the more hopeful or useful side of a hard situation without denying the difficulty. Parents model this in the language they use, and children learn to do it for themselves.

E stands for empathy. Many Danish schools set aside time to talk about feelings and friendships, and children are taught to understand others rather than judge them. Parents are urged to listen first and show children that their inner world matters.

N stands for no ultimatums. The authors favour calm, respectful discipline over shouting, threats and physical punishment. Power struggles shrink when parents stay steady, explain rules and treat children as people worth respecting.

T stands for togetherness and hygge, the Danish idea of cosy, relaxed time shared with others. Families light candles, cook, play and agree to set aside quarrels and complaints for a while, so home becomes a warm place where everyone belongs.
The book's message is hopeful: these are simple habits any family can begin to practise.

questions.q: What question prompted the authors to write the book?
options: Why Danish schools score highest in maths
Whether Denmark's high happiness levels are linked to how children are raised
How Danish parents earn more money
Why Danish families have fewer children
questions.why: They set out to explore whether Danish parenting helps explain Denmark's place near the top of happiness surveys.

questions.q: What does the word PARENT serve as in the book?
options: A checklist of school subjects
A daily timetable for children
An acronym organising the six key ideas
A list of rules for teenagers
questions.why: Each letter of PARENT stands for one of the book's main principles.

questions.q: Why do the authors value free, unstructured play?
options: It builds resilience, self-control and confidence
It keeps children quiet indoors
It prepares children for competitive sports
It reduces the need for school
questions.why: Free play lets children manage risks and conflicts, which strengthens coping skills.

questions.q: According to the authenticity principle, what kind of praise is encouraged?
options: Praise for being naturally clever
Praise only for winning
No praise at all
Praise for effort and the process of learning
questions.why: Focusing on effort helps children value growth rather than a fixed label.

questions.q: How does the book treat sad or difficult stories for children?
options: They should be hidden until adulthood
They should be shared, since facing real feelings is healthy
They should always be rewritten with happy endings
They should be told only by teachers
questions.why: Authenticity includes letting children meet and name sadness rather than avoiding it.

questions.q: What is meant by reframing in the book?
options: Pretending problems do not exist
Moving house to a new area
Finding the more hopeful or useful side of a situation while being realistic
Changing a child's school
questions.why: Reframing is realistic optimism, not denial of difficulty.

questions.q: How do many Danish schools support empathy, according to the authors?
options: By ranking pupils publicly
By banning group work
By giving extra homework
By setting aside time to talk about feelings and friendships
questions.why: Regular class time for discussing feelings helps children understand one another.

questions.q: What does the 'no ultimatums' principle recommend?
options: Calm, respectful discipline instead of threats and shouting
Strict punishments for every mistake
Letting children make all the rules
Avoiding any rules at all
questions.why: The authors argue that calm respect reduces power struggles better than threats.

options: A Danish school exam
Cosy, relaxed time shared together, setting quarrels aside
A type of outdoor sport
A strict family budget
questions.why: Hygge is about warm togetherness where everyone feels they belong.

questions.q: What is the book's overall message for families outside Denmark?
options: Only Danish families can raise happy children
Parents should move to Denmark
These are simple habits any family can begin to practise
Happiness depends mainly on wealth
questions.why: The authors present the PARENT ideas as everyday habits open to anyone.
